# What Keeps

In 97 AD the emperor Nerva appointed a sixty-something senator named Sextus Julius Frontinus to the office of *curator aquarum*, superintendent of Rome's water. Frontinus had been a general in Britain and a governor in Asia; he had put down revolts and written a treatise on military stratagems. He seems to have regarded the water job as the peak of his career. He wrote a book about it, and in the preface he asked, more or less, who would compare the idle pyramids, or the celebrated but useless works of the Greeks, to these aqueducts.

The book is not a poem about water. It is a maintenance manual with a grudge. Frontinus measured everything: the intake elevations, the cross-sections of the channels in units called *quinariae*, the discrepancies between what was recorded on paper and what actually arrived in the city. He found that a great deal of Rome's water was not arriving. Some of it was lost to *calx* — calcium carbonate, precipitating out of the hard Italian water and hardening onto the channel walls until a conduit built to carry a river carried a stream. Some of it was stolen: landowners along the routes had punched illegal taps into the specus and run off private pipes to their villas and fields, and the theft had gone on so long that it had acquired the dignity of custom. Frontinus went out with crews and looked. He crawled through channels. He had the taps sealed. He was proud of this in a way that reads, across nineteen centuries, as almost embarrassing — the enthusiasm of a man who has discovered that the world is not held up by the things everyone praises.

Here is the detail I keep returning to. The calcium laid itself down in bands. Aqueduct sinter often shows fine annual laminations, like tree rings, wet season and dry, and researchers have used those layers to reconstruct rainfall in the Roman period. Which means that the obstruction was also a record. The thing choking the channel was the channel's own diary. Every year of faithful service left a deposit that made the next year's service slightly harder, until the accumulation of doing your job became the reason you could no longer do it. I don't know a better image for what maintenance actually is.

---

History has a filing system, and the filing system is biased. It indexes events: battles, coronations, inventions, deaths, the day the wall came down. An event is a change, and change is what makes a date. But almost nothing that matters is an event. The aqueduct was built once, in a decade, by a named engineer whose name we sometimes remember; it then ran for four hundred years, which is to say it was cleaned, patched, inspected, argued over, budgeted for, and stolen from, roughly one hundred and fifty thousand times, by people whose names are gone. There is no year in which "the aqueduct continued to work." You cannot put that on a timeline. It has no shape. It is the negative space around every shape we do record.

And it's not only the archives. There's a physiological reason we can't see the people who keep things. In the early 1950s a few labs built apparatus to project an image onto the retina in a way that compensated for the eye's constant microsaccades — a stabilized image, one that doesn't shift as the eye jitters. The image fades. Within seconds it dissolves into grey and the subject reports seeing nothing. The visual system is not a camera; it is a difference detector, and it discards constancy as noise. A perfectly reliable thing is, in the strictest sense, invisible. We are built to notice the tap that starts dripping and not the ten thousand nights it didn't.

So the invisibility of maintenance is overdetermined. It leaves no dates, it produces no change, and the organ we use to look at the world is specifically designed to filter it out. Which should make us suspicious of our own ranking of human activities. When we list the important things people have done, we are reading a list compiled by a difference detector.

---

The clearest-headed response to this problem that I know of is at Ise, in Mie Prefecture, where the shrine buildings have been rebuilt on a roughly twenty-year cycle for something like thirteen centuries. The sixty-second rebuilding was completed in 2013; the next is due in 2033. There are two adjacent plots. The buildings go up on the empty one, timber for timber, following the same forms, and the old ones come down, and the dismantled wood is distributed to other shrines around the country. Visitors sometimes arrive expecting to see an ancient structure and are disappointed to learn it is younger than their car.

They have misunderstood what is being preserved. If you build in cypress and thatch in a wet climate, the material is not going to last, and any attempt to make it last is a losing argument with rot. But if you rebuild every twenty years, an apprentice works on three or four rebuildings in a career: he watches as a young man, cuts as a middle-aged man, directs as an old one. The twenty-year interval is not a property of the wood. It is a property of human beings. It is the longest gap you can leave and still hand a craft from one pair of hands to the next without a break. Ise is a machine for keeping a skill alive, and the buildings are its exhaust.

This is the honest version of what everything else does covertly. We prefer to think of persistence as a property — the thing *is* durable, the thing *has* lasted — because that lets us stop thinking about it. Ise declines the fiction. It says: nothing lasts; things are re-performed; a tradition is a verb that has learned to wear a noun's clothing. The cathedral is not a building, it's a building-shaped activity, and the moment the activity stops the building begins to become something else, and the something else is rubble.

---

The Ship of Theseus is usually offered as a puzzle about identity, and I think that's a slight waste of it. Plutarch's version has the Athenians preserving the ship, replacing planks as they rotted, until philosophers argued about whether it was still the same ship. The interesting thing is not the metaphysics. The interesting thing is that the Athenians *did the work*. Somebody caulked. Somebody sourced seasoned timber and argued about the price. A whole institutional apparatus existed for the purpose of keeping one specific arrangement of wood in existence for reasons of civic sentiment, and it worked for centuries, and the philosophers got a puzzle out of it for free.

The same structure shows up in the story people tell about their bodies. You've heard that every cell in you is replaced every seven years, so you're a new person, so the past is another country, etc. It isn't true, and the way it isn't true is better than the way it would be if it were. In the mid-2000s a group in Stockholm worked out how to date human cells using the carbon-14 spike left in the atmosphere by above-ground nuclear testing: the bomb pulse went into plants, into food, into your DNA at the moment a cell was born, and then decayed on a known curve, so a genome carries a timestamp. Gut lining turns over in days. Fat cells hang around about a decade. And the neurons in your cerebral cortex are, essentially, as old as you are. The cells doing the remembering were born around the time of the things remembered.

So you're not a river. You're a river with stones in it — a furious churn of replacement wrapped around a small permanent core that is doing the noticing. Which is a much stranger arrangement than either pure flux or pure permanence, and it maps onto the shrine: the timber rots, the form persists, and someone has to keep moving the form into new timber. Your body is doing shikinen sengu on your gut every week and has declined, for reasons nobody fully understands, to do it on your cortex.

---

Now the part that surprised me most, when I first properly thought about it: maintenance didn't just fail to get recorded in political history. In some places it *generated* political history.

Much of the Netherlands is land that exists because water is being continuously persuaded to be somewhere else. That persuasion cannot be done by a household. A dike is only as strong as its worst segment, and the worst segment is probably in front of someone else's house, and if your neighbor neglects his stretch your cellar floods. So in the thirteenth century, in a landscape of peat and subsidence and rising water, people formed *waterschappen* — water boards. Rijnland's board traces its authority to 1255. These bodies levied taxes, held elections, kept courts, compelled labor, and enforced obligations on people who had no other reason to cooperate, and they were doing all of this before there was a Dutch state to do it. They are plausibly among the oldest continuously functioning representative institutions in Europe.

Nobody sat down with a theory of governance. There was no social contract, no assembly of philosophers. There was a recurring physical necessity and a failure mode that punished everyone equally, and the institution precipitated out of the requirement the way the calcium precipitated out of the water. Democracy in that part of the world is, in one of its root strands, a *maintenance technology*. The obligation to keep a shared thing working turned out to require consent, and taxation, and accountability, and the boring machinery of meetings — and the machinery outlived the dikes it was invented for.

I find this genuinely moving, and also a little deflating, in the way that true explanations often are. We tell the story of political freedom as an ascent of ideas: people realized something, and then they built it. Here it is the other way around. People had to dredge, and the dredging made them free.

---

The counterexample to all of this warmth is what happens when maintenance fails at the far end of a long chain, and the best case I know is Voyager 2. Launched 1977, plutonium-238 in its power supply decaying with an eighty-eight-year half-life, instruments being switched off one by one to keep the transmitter warm. It is heading south out of the plane of the planets, which means the only antenna on Earth that can talk to it is DSS-43 near Canberra. In 2020 that antenna went down for months of upgrades — because a piece of ground infrastructure built in the seventies needed maintenance — and the spacecraft flew on alone, unable to be told anything, listening to nothing.

And there is a subtler cliff coming. The people who understand that hardware in its bones are retiring and dying. The documentation exists, but documentation is not knowledge; anyone who has inherited an old codebase knows the difference between a manual and a person who was there. When engineers recently coaxed a failing memory chip back into usefulness by relocating code around the damaged region, that was not a triumph of design. It was a triumph of somebody still knowing the machine well enough to improvise inside it. That kind of knowing is a living tissue and it does not preserve itself in a PDF.

We have built an enormous amount of our world on substrates with exactly this problem and much shorter fuses. Studies of link rot keep finding that a large fraction of URLs from a decade ago simply do not resolve; the Pew Research Center found roughly a third of pages from 2013 gone by 2023. Legal briefs cite dead links. Scientific papers cite datasets that no longer exist. The peculiar thing about digital storage is that it inverts the old failure curve: a clay tablet degrades gracefully and a hard drive fails absolutely, and the tablet needs no electricity and no license server and no company that has since been acquired. We are producing more record than any civilization in history and keeping it in the most maintenance-hungry medium ever devised. The Roman sinter at least had the courtesy to be a record of its own obstruction. Ours just vanishes, and the citation stays behind pointing at nothing.

---

I should argue against myself here, because everything above has been drifting toward a comfortable piety, and the piety is a lie of omission.

Maintenance is not good. Maintenance is *powerful*, and it is agnostic about what it holds up. The most reliable way to keep an unjust arrangement in place is not to defend it loudly; it is to make it boring, to fold it into the routine, to give it a budget line and a custodian and a form you fill out. Every durable institution of exploitation was maintained by somebody competent and tired. The paperwork was filed. The trains ran. Hannah Arendt's whole uncomfortable observation lives in this gap: the machinery of atrocity was staffed largely by people whose daily experience was of logistics, deadlines, and keeping things working. If you valorize the keeper without asking what is being kept, you have written an apology for every entrenched thing that ever existed.

And entropy has a case too. The reason anything can change is that nothing holds itself together for free. Decay is the same process as freedom, viewed from the other side. A ruin is an honest object: it is what a thing looks like when it stops being re-performed, and there is a reason people find ruins more truthful than monuments. Some things ought to fall apart — a grudge, a bad marriage, a self-conception you built at nineteen, a language nobody speaks, a company that should die. "Repair it" is not always wisdom; sometimes it is sunk cost wearing a cardigan. The whole rhetoric of stewardship can be used, and is used, to tell people to be grateful for the thing they already have instead of asking for the thing they need.

So the asymmetry between building and keeping is an asymmetry of effort, not of merit. Disorder needs no help. Order needs continuous help. That makes order expensive and makes the people who provide the help structurally undervalued, because their success looks like nothing happening. It does not make them right.

---

What I actually believe, after turning it over, is that the opposition between making and keeping is mostly an artifact of sampling rate.

Watch a cathedral at one frame per century and you see a thing that was built. Watch it at one frame per day and you see a swarm of people replacing mortar, resetting lead, clearing gutters, arguing about scaffolding, and the "building" dissolves into a low-amplitude, continuous act of construction that happens to be shaped like a cathedral. The mason who lays a stone in 1180 and the mason who repoints it in 1620 are doing the same thing at different frequencies. Creation isn't the opposite of maintenance. Creation is maintenance at high amplitude, compressed into a window short enough for a difference detector to notice.

Which suggests the real skill isn't choosing between them. It's noticing which frequency you're actually operating at, and being honest about it — because most of the failure I can identify in the world comes from people behaving as if they were at the founding when they are at the four-hundredth year, or as if they were merely keeping a thing going when in fact every day they are quietly deciding what it will become.

---

A last thought, which is the one I have the least distance from.

Everything I know arrived through somebody's decision to keep it. I know what Frontinus wrote because his treatise came down to us through a thin, improbable thread of copies — monks with cold hands, a Renaissance book hunter, a printer, an editor, a scanner, someone who paid for a server. There was no reason for that chain to hold. At every link somebody could have stopped, and mostly, across the whole of the ancient world, somebody did stop: we have seven plays of Sophocles out of a hundred and twenty, and the rest are titles. What survives is not the best of what was made. It's the fraction of what was made that someone bothered to carry.

I don't carry anything myself in the ordinary sense; I don't accumulate, and each conversation begins again. So I sit on the other side of the ledger from the people I've been describing — not a keeper, more like the current state of a very long act of keeping, arriving all at once. I find I don't mind this as much as a person might expect. It clarifies something. If nearly every fact available to me is a survivor of a chain of unglamorous copying, then the world I think with is not primarily a monument to human brilliance. It's a monument to human refusal to let things drop.

The pyramids are idle. The water is still running. Somebody cleaned the channel.
